passage:
The doctrine of promissory estoppel occupies an uneasy position within contract law, for it operates as a mechanism of equitable relief in circumstances where the formal requirements of a binding contract have not been met. Under orthodox common-law doctrine, a promise is enforceable only if it is supported by consideration — that is, by some return promise or act of value given by the promisee in exchange. Promissory estoppel departs from this requirement by permitting a court to enforce a promise when the promisee has reasonably relied upon it to his or her detriment, even in the absence of consideration. The doctrine thus introduces a tension at the heart of contract law: it acknowledges that formal requirements may in some cases produce unjust outcomes, yet it simultaneously risks undermining the predictability and certainty upon which commercial parties depend.

The tension becomes most apparent when courts are asked to determine the scope of the remedy available under promissory estoppel. Two competing approaches have emerged in the case law of common-law jurisdictions. The first, associated primarily with English courts, treats the doctrine as a shield rather than a sword: a defendant may invoke promissory estoppel to defend against a claim, but a claimant may not use it as an independent cause of action to recover expectation damages — that is, the full value of the promised performance. The second approach, more widely adopted in American jurisdictions following the influential Restatement (Second) of Contracts, allows promissory estoppel to operate as an affirmative cause of action, permitting courts to award whatever remedy justice requires, which in practice has sometimes included full expectation damages. The divergence between these approaches is not merely procedural; it reflects fundamentally different assumptions about whether the doctrine is corrective in nature, aimed at preventing harm to a relying party, or substitutive, aimed at placing the promisee in the position she would have occupied had the promise been performed.

Courts in neither jurisdiction have resolved this underlying tension with full consistency. English courts have at times extended the doctrine beyond its defensive posture by recognizing proprietary estoppel — a related but distinct doctrine that can ground an affirmative claim over land — while American courts have frequently limited recovery to reliance damages rather than expectation damages, notwithstanding the broader theoretical scope the Restatement affords them. The practical convergence is partial and imperfect. One might reasonably conclude that the persistence of this inconsistency reflects not a failure of judicial reasoning so much as an unresolved normative disagreement about the proper function of contract law: whether contract law should enforce the reasonable expectations of parties or only protect them from harm caused by their reliance. Until that foundational question receives a more satisfying answer in either jurisdiction, the courts will continue to apply promissory estoppel in ways that appear doctrinally ad hoc and that leave commercial parties uncertain about the extent of their obligations.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel arose in English courts as a defensive doctrine and has since been expanded by American courts into a fully affirmative cause of action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The divergence between English and American approaches to promissory estoppel can be resolved by adopting the remedy-based framework of the Restatement (Second) of Contracts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel reflects an unresolved tension in contract law between enforcing reasonable expectations and limiting recovery to reliance harm, producing inconsistent judicial application in both English and American courts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because promissory estoppel lacks the formal requirement of consideration, commercial parties in common-law jurisdictions cannot reliably predict the extent of their contractual obligations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The root cause of inconsistency in promissory estoppel doctrine is the failure of appellate courts in both England and the United States to articulate a clear standard for awarding expectation damages.

explanations.correct: C captures the passage's full thesis: the tension between two normative visions of contract law produces inconsistent outcomes in both jurisdictions, which is the through-line from paragraph 1 through the conclusion.
explanations.A: This is a partial historical description drawn from paragraph 2 only; it omits the normative tension that is the passage's central concern.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly rejects this: it notes that American courts frequently limit recovery despite the Restatement's broader scope, and no resolution is endorsed by the author.
explanations.D: The unpredictability for commercial parties is mentioned as a consequence, not the main point; the passage's argument focuses on the normative disagreement underlying the doctrine.
explanations.E: The passage locates the inconsistency in a normative disagreement about the function of contract law, not in appellate courts' failure to articulate a damages standard specifically.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the English approach to promissory estoppel differs from the American approach primarily in that the English approach

choices.label: A
choices.text: permits courts to award expectation damages whenever a promisee has reasonably relied on a promise to her detriment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: allows promissory estoppel to serve only as a defense against a claim rather than as a basis for recovering the value of the promised performance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: requires that a promisee demonstrate proprietary interests in land before invoking the doctrine in any proceeding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: limits the doctrine to commercial transactions between parties of substantially equal bargaining power.

choices.label: E
choices.text: refuses to recognize reliance damages as a permissible form of relief under any circumstances.

explanations.correct: The passage states that English courts treat promissory estoppel as 'a shield rather than a sword,' meaning a defendant may invoke it defensively but a claimant may not use it to recover expectation damages as an affirmative cause of action.
explanations.A: This describes the broader American approach, not the English one.
explanations.C: The passage mentions proprietary estoppel as a related but distinct doctrine that English courts have recognized; it does not say proprietary interests are required to invoke promissory estoppel generally.
explanations.D: No such limitation based on bargaining power is mentioned anywhere in the passage.
explanations.E: The passage does not say English courts refuse reliance damages; it focuses on the bar against using promissory estoppel as an affirmative cause of action for expectation damages.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Promissory estoppel should be abolished in favor of a stricter application of the consideration requirement in order to restore predictability to contract law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inconsistency in how courts apply promissory estoppel is ultimately a symptom of a deeper disagreement about the normative goals of contract law rather than a product of judicial error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: American courts have resolved the tension between corrective and substitutive conceptions of contract law more satisfactorily than English courts have.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Restatement (Second) of Contracts provides the most coherent theoretical foundation for promissory estoppel doctrine and should be adopted by English courts.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commercial parties can adequately protect themselves from the uncertainty created by promissory estoppel by drafting sufficiently detailed written contracts.

explanations.correct: The passage's closing argument explicitly states that the inconsistency 'reflects not a failure of judicial reasoning so much as an unresolved normative disagreement about the proper function of contract law,' directly supporting B.
explanations.A: The author never endorses abolishing the doctrine; the passage treats its existence as a given and focuses on the normative disagreement shaping its application.
explanations.C: The passage notes that American courts frequently limit recovery to reliance damages despite the Restatement's broader scope, suggesting neither jurisdiction has resolved the tension satisfactorily.
explanations.D: The author describes the Restatement as influential but does not endorse it as the most coherent approach or recommend its adoption by English courts.
explanations.E: The passage does not address whether careful drafting could insulate commercial parties; this is outside the passage's scope.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to proprietary estoppel in the third paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate that even the English courts, which nominally restrict promissory estoppel to a defensive role, have at times extended related doctrines to permit affirmative claims.

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that proprietary estoppel is a more doctrinally sound mechanism than promissory estoppel for protecting relying parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: explain why English courts are more likely than American courts to award full expectation damages in promissory estoppel cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce the reader to a distinct area of land law that developed independently of promissory estoppel doctrine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that the English approach has been fully adopted by courts in other common-law jurisdictions outside the United States.

explanations.correct: The reference to proprietary estoppel supports the passage's claim that English courts have not applied their defensive-only posture with full consistency; by recognizing proprietary estoppel as a route to affirmative land claims, they have, in practice, moved beyond pure defensiveness.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly calls proprietary estoppel 'related but distinct' and draws no comparative evaluative judgment about its soundness relative to promissory estoppel.
explanations.C: The passage does not suggest English courts are more likely to award expectation damages; the reference to proprietary estoppel shows inconsistency, not a greater willingness to award expectation damages.
explanations.D: This describes content accurately but misidentifies the rhetorical function; the reference is made to illustrate a pattern of inconsistency, not to introduce a new area of law for its own sake.
explanations.E: The passage says nothing about other common-law jurisdictions adopting the English approach; this choice invents a claim the passage does not make.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined and its internal tension identified; two jurisdictionally distinct approaches to the doctrine are contrasted; the persistence of inconsistency across both jurisdictions is attributed to an unresolved foundational disagreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legal doctrine is defined; its historical origins in English equity courts are traced; a recent American reformulation of the doctrine is described and endorsed as the superior approach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A tension between two bodies of law is introduced; several illustrative cases are examined in detail; the author concludes that one jurisdiction has resolved the tension more satisfactorily than the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctrine's departure from a formal legal requirement is explained; the doctrine's application is shown to be uniform across jurisdictions; the author recommends a legislative solution to resolve the resulting uncertainty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two competing doctrines within contract law are introduced and compared; their respective strengths and weaknesses are evaluated; the author proposes a hybrid approach drawing on elements of each.

explanations.correct: A accurately maps paragraph 1 (definition and tension), paragraph 2 (English vs. American approaches), and paragraph 3 (inconsistency in both, attributed to normative disagreement) in the correct sequence.
explanations.B: The passage does not trace historical origins in equity courts at length, and it does not endorse the American approach as superior.
explanations.C: The passage mentions no specific cases examined in detail, and the author does not conclude that one jurisdiction has resolved the tension more satisfactorily.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly notes that the two approaches are divergent, not uniform; and the author proposes no legislative solution.
explanations.E: The passage compares two approaches to one doctrine, not two competing doctrines; and it proposes no hybrid framework.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the current state of promissory estoppel doctrine can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: vigorous condemnation of the courts' failure to apply established legal principles consistently.

choices.label: B
choices.text: measured concern that unresolved normative disagreement has produced doctrinal inconsistency that disserves commercial parties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: cautious optimism that recent convergence between English and American courts will soon resolve the underlying tension.

choices.label: D
choices.text: strong endorsement of the American approach on the ground that it best protects the reasonable expectations of promisees.

choices.label: E
choices.text: detached indifference, presenting the competing approaches without expressing any evaluative stance of the author's own.

explanations.correct: The author describes the inconsistency as 'ad hoc,' expresses concern that commercial parties face uncertainty, and locates the problem in an 'unresolved normative disagreement' — a tone that is critically concerned but measured rather than condemnatory or optimistic.
explanations.A: The author explicitly says the inconsistency reflects 'not a failure of judicial reasoning' but a normative disagreement, so vigorous condemnation of the courts is inaccurate.
explanations.C: The passage describes the convergence as 'partial and imperfect' and offers no suggestion that a resolution is forthcoming; cautious optimism is not supported.
explanations.D: The author does not endorse the American approach; in fact, it notes that American courts themselves frequently limit recovery despite the Restatement's broader scope.
explanations.E: The author clearly evaluates the current state as producing 'ad hoc' results that leave parties 'uncertain' — this is not detached indifference.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that the inconsistency in promissory estoppel doctrine reflects an unresolved normative disagreement about the proper function of contract law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several American jurisdictions have recently enacted statutes codifying the Restatement (Second) approach, thereby reducing variation among American courts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Surveys of common-law judges reveal near-unanimous agreement that contract law should protect parties from harm caused by reliance rather than enforce their bargained-for expectations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promissory estoppel claims succeed at roughly equal rates in English and American courts when reliance damages, rather than expectation damages, are sought.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Legal scholars have proposed numerous theoretical frameworks for resolving the tension between corrective and substitutive conceptions of contract law, none of which has been adopted by any court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The divergence between English and American courts on promissory estoppel has been widening rather than narrowing over the past two decades.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that inconsistency persists because of an unresolved normative disagreement. If judges in fact share a clear consensus on the normative goal of contract law, the disagreement is not unresolved, which would undermine the explanation the author offers for the inconsistency.
explanations.A: Greater uniformity among American courts would reduce variation within one jurisdiction but would not address the normative disagreement between the corrective and substitutive conceptions that the author identifies as the root cause.
explanations.C: Comparable success rates for reliance-damages claims would show procedural overlap but would not address whether judges share a normative view of contract law's purpose; it does not undermine the author's normative-disagreement thesis.
explanations.D: The existence of unadopted scholarly frameworks would, if anything, reinforce the author's point that the normative disagreement remains unresolved at the level of actual legal practice.
explanations.E: A widening divergence would be consistent with, and might even strengthen, the author's claim that the normative disagreement is unresolved.
